title: Cqlib: A High-Performance Software Stack for Quantum Computing
authors: Tianyan Quantum Group
abstract: This paper presents Cqlib, a high-performance software stack for quantum computing built around a unified quantum circuit model. Its native Rust core provides efficient implementations of circuit processing, quantum-state and operator computation, compilation, and optimization, while Python and C interfaces support algorithm development and system integration. Cqlib covers quantum program construction, simulation, analysis, compilation, device adaptation, and result processing under consistent program semantics. Through OpenQASM and the Quantum Control Instruction Set (QCIS), Cqlib supports program representation and hardware-oriented execution. Cqlib further provides backend interfaces for device execution, with Cqlib-Tianyan serving as one implementation for QCIS-compatible quantum hardware. Evaluations using parameterized compilation tasks from Benchpress and related tests show that Cqlib achieves good functional coverage, compilation correctness, and execution efficiency within the evaluated task scope. We develop Cqlib-Algorithm as a modular library of reusable operators and composable components for widely used quantum algorithms, including quantum search, phase estimation, and variational algorithms, with additional support for error mitigation. To complement these building blocks with domain-specific workflows, we further develop Cqlib-VQE, Cqlib-QAOA, and Cqlib-QML for application-level studies in quantum chemistry, combinatorial optimization, and quantum machine learning, respectively. Cqlib also integrates source-grounded Skills and MCP-based tools to support agent-assisted program generation, backend execution, and result-guided workflow refinement. Overall, Cqlib provides a unified and extensible software foundation that connects quantum algorithm development, simulation, compilation, and execution on QCIS-compatible quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: Cqlib unifies quantum program development, simulation, compilation, and hardware execution around a shared circuit model and a high-performance Rust core.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Python and C interfaces, reusable algorithm libraries, and QCIS-compatible backend integration support end-to-end quantum computing workflows.
method: Use consistent circuit semantics across processing, simulation, optimization, and compilation.
Connect OpenQASM and QCIS representations to device backends and domain-specific application libraries.
Integrate source-grounded Skills and MCP tools for agent-assisted generation, execution, and workflow refinement.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchpress parameterized compilation tasks and related tests indicate functional coverage, compilation correctness, and execution efficiency within the evaluated scope; the abstract reports no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Performance and portability beyond the evaluated tasks and QCIS-compatible hardware remain unestablished by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Cqlib: A High-Performance Software Stack for Quantum Computing

title: Machine Learning-Based Quantum Error Mitigation for Bound-State Simulations
authors: Sumit Choudhary, Tarunpreet Kaur, Harjeet Kaur, Harpreet Singh
abstract: Noise in quantum devices remains a major challenge for reliable quantum simulations, making quantum error mitigation an important tool for improving their accuracy. Machine learning-based quantum error mitigation (ML-QEM) provides a useful approach, but its performance depends on the training datasets and may produce reconstructed quantum states that are not physically valid. In this work, we introduce an ML-QEM framework that uses residual learning with convex projection to ensure that reconstructed density matrices satisfy physically valid density matrices. We study the effect of different training datasets and regression models using Haar-random and variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) ansatz states. We compare the proposed approach with conventional ML-QEM, readout error mitigation, and zero-noise extrapolation. The method is tested on IBM quantum hardware for three- and four-qubit simulations of the bound $Λ$-deuteron and $Λ$-$α$ hypernuclear systems, respectively. For the three-qubit system, ridge regression trained on VQE-ansatz states gives a ground-state energy of -0.134 MeV, close to the ideal value of -0.135 MeV, with a state fidelity of 0.999. For four-qubit system, kernel ridge regression gives ground-state energies of -3.014 and -3.045 MeV, with corresponding state fidelities of 0.995 and 0.998. These results show that physically constrained reconstruction, along with the choice of training datasets and regression models, can improve ML-QEM performance for the quantum simulations studied in this work.

infographic.key_insight: Residual learning with convex projection improves machine learning-based quantum error mitigation while ensuring reconstructed density matrices are physically valid.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework can improve noisy-hardware bound-state simulations, with performance depending on the training states and regression model.
method: Use residual learning to reconstruct noise-mitigated quantum states.
Apply convex projection to enforce density-matrix physicality.
Evaluate Haar-random versus VQE-ansatz training states and compare against conventional ML-QEM, readout mitigation, and zero-noise extrapolation.
infographic.evidence_signal: IBM hardware tests on three- and four-qubit hypernuclear systems achieved a three-qubit energy of −0.134 MeV versus the ideal −0.135 MeV with 0.999 fidelity, and four-qubit energies of −3.014 and −3.045 MeV with fidelities of 0.995 and 0.998.
infographic.watch_item: Results are limited to small systems; scalability and robustness across different noise conditions remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Machine Learning-Based Quantum Error Mitigation for Bound-State Simulations

title: Non unitary and nonlinear quantum generative large model design and fast large-scale training without back propagation
authors: Tianze Zhu, Xiaofeng Jiang, Min Liao, Luying Zhang, Ruixi Liu, Sen Kuang
abstract: Transformer-based large models require huge computational and storage costs. Quantum computation is expected to address that due to its potential to speed up classical algorithms exponentially. Key challenges of implementing quantum large models include the linear, unitary nature of qubit evolutions contrast with the non-unitary matrices and nonlinear functions in classical Transformers, as well as the difficulty of implementing gradient back-propagation on quantum hardware. Here we propose a fully quantum large model containing all the Transformer layers, implementing the non-unitary transformations through SVD-decomposition-based quantum circuits, and approximated nonlinear activation functions through pre-trained parameterized quantum circuits. We also propose a quantum circuit training algorithm based on multi-agent Reinforcement Learning, which can train large-scale parameterized quantum circuits without back-propagation. The dependency between the inference time complexity and the model's hidden dimension has been reduced from polynomial to logarithmic, showing an exponential advantage. The inference executions on the quantum hardware verify our model's 300-1000 times speed-up, and the measurements on the sequence-to-sequence tasks shows its learning ability. The training algorithm achieves only 25% complexity of the best SOTA quantum circuit training algorithms, especially this ratio decreases fast as the parameter scale increases. Our work not only proposes a quantum large model that can significantly reduce the computational cost, but also promotes the quantum computation towards general computing.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes a fully quantum Transformer with non-unitary and approximate nonlinear operations, claiming logarithmic rather than polynomial inference scaling in hidden dimension.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The design targets lower inference costs and backpropagation-free training for large parameterized quantum circuits.
method: Implement non-unitary transformations using SVD-based quantum circuits.
Approximate nonlinear activations with pretrained parameterized quantum circuits.
Train quantum circuits using multi-agent reinforcement learning without backpropagation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 300–1000× inference speedups on quantum hardware, learning on sequence-to-sequence tasks, and training complexity at 25% of the best compared quantum training methods.
infographic.watch_item: Practical advantage requires scrutiny of comparison baselines, hardware noise, state-preparation and readout costs, and nonlinear approximation error, which the abstract does not detail.
infographic.paper_title: Non unitary and nonlinear quantum generative large model design and fast large-scale training without back propagation

title: Solving the Traveling Salesman Problem Using Quantum Devices: QUBO and HOBO Formulations
authors: G. V. Shuvalov, E. N. Krivtsova, A. V. Kapranov, M. A. Remnev
abstract: The traveling salesman problem (TSP) forms the foundation for many logistics and optimization tasks. At the same time, this problem is NP-hard and requires significant computational resources. Quantum computing promises to substantially accelerate computations or increase solution accuracy. The TSP can be conveniently mapped onto the quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) formulation, which in turn can be solved using variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) and quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) methods, but this mapping requires a quadratic number of qubits. The higher-order binary optimization (HOBO) formulation requires significantly fewer qubits, but it contains higher-order terms. In our work, we thoroughly investigate both formulations and provide a practical recipe for solving the TSP. We give a comprehensive study and compare in detail QUBO and HOBO formulations.

infographic.key_insight: For quantum approaches to the traveling salesman problem, QUBO requires quadratically many qubits, while HOBO reduces qubit requirements by introducing higher-order terms.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The comparison helps engineers weigh qubit availability against interaction complexity when selecting a quantum optimization formulation.
method: Map the traveling salesman problem to QUBO and HOBO formulations.
Investigate quantum solution approaches, including VQE and QAOA.
Compare the formulations and provide a practical solution recipe.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a detailed comparative study but provides no numerical benchmarks, instance sizes, or measured performance gains.
infographic.watch_item: HOBO's lower qubit count does not guarantee easier implementation because higher-order terms may complicate execution on quantum hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Solving the Traveling Salesman Problem Using Quantum Devices: QUBO and HOBO Formulations

title: Observable-Level Expressivity in Fixed-Readout Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Iqra Bashir, Yuanfeng Wang, Mingda Huang, Keren Li, Qi Qin
abstract: A central question in quantum machine learning is which functions of an input state a model can represent when its measurement is fixed by hardware or by experimental design. We address this question for quantum neural networks with a fixed readout observable, where the trainable pre-measurement dynamics determine the effective observable in the Heisenberg picture and the scalar output is the measured expectation value itself, without trainable affine post-processing. We characterize the reachable effective observables under three physical resource classes: unitary evolution, which preserves the spectrum of the readout; mixed-unitary evolution, which relaxes this to a majorization constraint while preserving the trace; and completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) evolution, whose Heisenberg adjoint is unital rather than trace-preserving and therefore lifts the trace constraint inherited at the mixed-unitary level. The three reachable sets are a fixed-spectrum orbit, its convex hull, and an operator interval, and the inclusions are strict for any readout that is not proportional to the identity. The separation is witnessed locally: for a fixed Pauli readout $Z_j$ on an arbitrary number of qubits, the amplitude-damping observable $γ\id+(1-γ)Z_j$ lies outside the mixed-unitary level for every $γ>0$. We realize the CPTP level with a Stinespring-channelized circuit and derive closed-form loss floors, $4γ^2/3$ and $γ^2$ for the unitary and mixed-unitary levels and zero at the CPTP level, which the numerics reproduce within precision. Structured-observable, Rényi-moment and classification experiments illustrate how the hierarchy manifests in finite-depth ansätze. The results identify which spectral constraint each physical resource relaxes, framing reachable-observable classes as a resource for expressivity rather than an architectural advantage.

infographic.key_insight: With fixed measurement and no trainable affine output processing, reachable observables expand strictly from a fixed-spectrum unitary orbit to its mixed-unitary convex hull to a CPTP operator interval for any nonconstant readout.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The hierarchy identifies when adding general quantum channels can overcome expressivity limits that deeper unitary circuits cannot remove.
method: Characterize effective Heisenberg-picture observables under unitary, mixed-unitary, and CPTP dynamics.
Use amplitude damping with a fixed Pauli readout to demonstrate separation from mixed-unitary models.
Implement CPTP dynamics through a Stinespring-channelized circuit and derive analytic loss floors.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerics reproduce loss floors of 4γ²/3, γ², and zero for the unitary, mixed-unitary, and CPTP levels, respectively; structured-observable, Rényi-moment, and classification experiments illustrate finite-depth behavior.
infographic.watch_item: The reachable-set hierarchy does not guarantee that finite-depth channel circuits can efficiently train to the optimal observable.
infographic.paper_title: Observable-Level Expressivity in Fixed-Readout Quantum Neural Networks

title: Thermal state preparation with shallow quantum circuits
authors: Cenk Tüysüz, Simon Deconihout, Enrico Rinaldi, Michele Grossi
abstract: Preparing thermal states on noisy quantum hardware requires circuits that remain shallow at low temperatures. Even when accurate classical state representations are available, compiling them into suitable circuits can be costly. We introduce PP-VarQITE, combining Pauli propagation with variational quantum imaginary-time evolution to determine circuit parameters entirely classically, with target temperatures encoded in the angles of a fixed circuit architecture. In numerical studies of Ising and frustrated Heisenberg models, we recover low-temperature energies and correlations using up to 100 qubits. Across the frustrated chain and two-dimensional lattice, our circuits are approximately two to ten times shallower than the lowest-depth circuits from sequential tensor-network compilation. These shallow circuits enable us to prepare a 48-site frustrated chain and a $7\times7$ Ising lattice using 96 and 98 qubits on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum processor. We reproduce the development of dimer order and lattice-wide correlations from high to low temperatures, with the lattice circuits requiring at most 42 two-qubit layers. Through classical circuit design, we demonstrate low-temperature state preparation at circuit sizes beyond the practical reach of statevector simulation.

infographic.key_insight: PP-VarQITE designs shallow thermal-state preparation circuits entirely classically, encoding temperature in the angles of a fixed circuit architecture.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reducing circuit depth makes low-temperature quantum simulation more practical on noisy hardware without requiring quantum measurements during parameter optimization.
method: Combine Pauli propagation with variational quantum imaginary-time evolution.
Determine temperature-dependent circuit parameters entirely classically.
Execute the resulting shallow circuits on trapped-ion hardware.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical tests reached 100 qubits and yielded circuits approximately 2–10× shallower than sequential tensor-network compilation baselines; Quantinuum Helios experiments used 96 and 98 qubits, with the Ising lattice requiring at most 42 two-qubit layers.
infographic.watch_item: The reported depth advantage is model- and baseline-specific; classical optimization costs and robustness on other hardware require further evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Thermal state preparation with shallow quantum circuits

title: A machine learning architecture for scaling of holographic quantum circuits
authors: Cliff Sun, Michael L. Wall
abstract: We describe an architecture and workflow for learning and generalizing the syntax and parameters of holographic quantum circuits (HQCs), which are natural quantum circuit analogs of classical tensor networks. An HQC uses mid-circuit measurements and resets on a small subset of "physical" qubits whose measurement outcomes become correlated through coupling with a register of persistent "ancilla" qubits, analogous to the physical and bond indices of a tensor network. Hence, an HQC with fixed qubit resources can efficiently generate samples from a large quantum state, and adding qubits to the HQC ansatz has the effect of exponentially increasing the effective bond dimension. Our machine learning approach provides mechanisms for harnessing both features of HQCs by extrapolating the syntax (e.g., a sequence of gates, measurements, and resets) and parameters (e.g., the angles appearing in single-qubit rotations) from a dataset of HQCs to longer or more expressive HQCs. We demonstrate the methodology and its performance on an analytically solvable dataset formed by a vector-valued generalization of the W-state. Finally, we provide an outlook for usage of the methodology for scaling the effective bond dimensions of HQCs in quantum simulation.

infographic.key_insight: A machine learning architecture learns holographic quantum circuit syntax and parameters to extrapolate to longer or more expressive circuits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reusing measured and reset qubits supports sampling large quantum states with fixed qubit resources, while adding qubits exponentially increases the effective bond dimension.
method: Encode states using reusable physical qubits coupled to persistent ancilla qubits.
Learn gate, measurement, and reset sequences alongside rotation parameters from circuit datasets.
Extrapolate learned syntax and parameters to larger circuit instances.
infographic.evidence_signal: The methodology is demonstrated on an analytically solvable dataset based on a vector-valued generalization of the W-state; the abstract reports no quantitative performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond the solvable dataset and practical performance under hardware noise remain unestablished in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: A machine learning architecture for scaling of holographic quantum circuits

title: Binary-Tree Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm for the Maximum $k$-Cut Problem
authors: Zhaoyang Song, Wei Zhang, Ji Cao, Xuexi Yi, Hong-Fu Wang
abstract: The maximum $k$-cut (Max-$k$-Cut) problem, as a natural generalization of the maximum-cut (MaxCut) problem, has broader applications in practical engineering. To solve this problem on quantum devices, existing studies typically encode the $k$ possible subset assignments of each vertex within the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), which directly causes the required quantum resources to grow substantially with $k$. Here we propose a binary-tree quantum approximate optimization algorithm (BT-QAOA), which solves the Max-$k$-Cut problem by applying standard MaxCut QAOA to at most $2k-3$ subproblems. Specifically, after solving MaxCut once on the full vertex set, each subsequent step splits only the subset that yields the largest cut-value gain. This process is equivalent to constructing a binary tree whose leaf nodes after $k-1$ steps form an approximate solution to the Max-$k$-Cut problem. Furthermore, we derive a theoretical lower bound on the approximation ratio in terms of the single-step splitting quality, showing that the overall approximation ratio does not decay exponentially across multiple splits. Numerical simulations show that BT-QAOA substantially reduces the single-circuit qubit and gate overhead while maintaining a high approximation ratio, improving the estimated success probability of a single compiled circuit by orders of magnitude. This work effectively expands the practical reach of QAOA on near-term quantum hardware, offering a new route for solving more complex real-world optimization problems with limited quantum resources.

infographic.key_insight: BT-QAOA approximates Max-k-Cut through binary-tree partitioning with standard MaxCut QAOA, reducing per-circuit resource demands without directly encoding k assignments per vertex.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could make multiway graph-partitioning optimization more accessible on qubit- and gate-limited quantum hardware.
method: Run standard MaxCut QAOA on the full vertex set.
Repeatedly split the subset with the largest estimated cut-value gain, using at most 2k−3 MaxCut subproblems overall.
After k−1 splits, use the tree’s k leaves as the partition.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical simulations report lower per-circuit qubit and gate overhead, high approximation ratios, and orders-of-magnitude improvements in estimated single-compiled-circuit success probability.
infographic.watch_item: Per-circuit savings require multiple subproblem solves; the abstract does not establish end-to-end runtime gains or hardware-validated performance.
infographic.paper_title: Binary-Tree Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm for the Maximum $k$-Cut Problem

title: Blueprint for DOE Quantum Supercomputing
authors: Ryan Bennink, Robin Blume-Kohout, Salman Habib, Andrew Landahl, Hai Ah Nam, Laura Schulz
abstract: Quantum computing stands at the threshold of a transformative decade, where the field will evolve from small-scale demonstrations toward practical scientific computing at scale. This Blueprint identifies fault-tolerant quantum computers (FTQCs) as a viable, scalable, and broadly applicable path to achieving "quantum scientific utility." It outlines a strategy to prepare the US Department of Energy (DOE) for FTQCs and their integration into the US national scientific computing infrastructure. Its purpose is to identify the steps, milestones, and research directions necessary for DOE to enable initial deployment of FTQCs in 2028 as a scientific tool for the nation and mature this capability into the 2030s. Given recent demonstrations of logical operations on error-corrected logical qubits and the advancement of commercial hardware roadmaps, DOE should begin preparations for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing deployment for DOE science missions. This Blueprint proposes that DOE focus on (1) deploying first-generation scientifically relevant quantum computers with at least 100 logical qubits and performing at least 10,000 to 100,000 hard logical operations in scientifically relevant calculations; (2) developing essential FTQC programming competencies, system software, and facility readiness; and (3) investing in cutting-edge focused R&D that fosters breakthroughs in scientific applications, algorithms, and logical architectures needed to accelerate the advent of scientific utility. This effort will position DOE to transition to larger systems: production-scale quantum computers that comprise 1,000 to 10,000 logical qubits, perform 1 to 10 billion hard logical operations, and execute scientifically useful computations at scale. The Blueprint calls for transformative R&D and collective action to accelerate the advent of scientific quantum utility and bring it within reach by 2028.

infographic.key_insight: The Blueprint proposes preparing DOE to deploy fault-tolerant quantum computers for scientific use beginning in 2028 and scale capabilities through the 2030s.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Integrating quantum computers into national scientific computing infrastructure requires coordinated development of error-corrected hardware, programming tools, system software, and facility readiness.
method: Target first-generation systems with at least 100 logical qubits and 10,000–100,000 hard logical operations per scientifically relevant calculation.
Build FTQC programming competencies, system software, and deployment-ready facilities.
Invest in applications, algorithms, and logical architectures to enable production-scale systems.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract cites recent error-corrected logical-operation demonstrations and commercial hardware roadmaps as motivation, but reports no new benchmarks validating the proposed deployment targets.
infographic.watch_item: Scientific utility by 2028 remains a strategic goal, contingent on hardware scaling, reliable logical operations, and successful infrastructure integration.
infographic.paper_title: Blueprint for DOE Quantum Supercomputing

title: Prospects and limitations of adaptive variational quantum algorithms for lattice field theories: a case study in 2+1 dimensions
authors: Nico Dichter, Andrea Bulgarelli, Lena Funcke, Stefan Kühn
abstract: The variational quantum algorithm ADAPT-VQE has previously been used to prepare the vacuum of lattice gauge theories in $1+1D$. In this paper, we study whether it extends to higher dimensions. We identify two general limitations of ADAPT-VQE. First, if the qubit Hamiltonian and the initial state are real, i.e., invariant under qubit-level time-reversal, all real-valued pool operators have vanishing gradients and are never selected. Second, the algorithm can converge to excited eigenstates. We illustrate both limitations, also providing examples from literature, and present a first application of ADAPT-VQE to a lattice field theory in $2+1D$, namely free Wilson fermions, where both obstacles occur. Adding charge conjugation symmetry to the operator pool improves the results, and combining different pools with suitable initial states recovers the ground and first excited states over the full mass range. These findings give practical guidelines for applying ADAPT-VQE to lattice field theories beyond $1+1D$.

infographic.key_insight: ADAPT-VQE faces symmetry-induced zero gradients and excited-state convergence, but suitable operator pools and initial states can recover target states in a 2+1D lattice field theory.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable lattice-field state preparation requires designing operator pools and initial states around symmetries rather than relying on adaptive energy minimization alone.
method: Analyze vanishing gradients for real-valued pool operators when the qubit Hamiltonian and initial state are real.
Apply ADAPT-VQE to free Wilson fermions in 2+1 dimensions.
Incorporate charge-conjugation symmetry and combine different pools with suitable initial states.
infographic.evidence_signal: The free-Wilson-fermion case exhibits both failure modes, while tailored pool–initial-state combinations recover the ground and first excited states across the full mass range studied.
infographic.watch_item: Success in this free-fermion case does not establish scalability or reliability for interacting higher-dimensional lattice gauge theories.
infographic.paper_title: Prospects and limitations of adaptive variational quantum algorithms for lattice field theories: a case study in 2+1 dimensions

title: Quantum optimization beyond qubit count by low-energy subspace sampling
authors: Mateo Alonso, Gonzalo Blázquez-Gil, Pablo Díez-Valle
abstract: On current digital quantum devices, standard one-qubit-per-variable encodings restrict quantum optimization algorithms to problem sizes where classical solvers typically excel. To avoid this constraint, we introduce Quantum Subspace Sampling Descent (QSSD), an iterative heuristic that decouples the number of problem variables from qubit count, while preserving knowledge of the problem's global structure. QSSD drives the energy descent using a fixed-angle Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm as a low-energy sampler. As the angles are precomputed, each iteration requires just a single circuit execution. We test QSSD on IBM Heron and Nighthawk quantum devices with up to 152 qubits on instances of higher-order unconstrained binary optimization and Max-cut problems. On the largest instance with 10000 variables, QSSD reaches an approximation ratio above 0.95 with 100 circuit executions. We provide both exact and heuristic classical baselines, namely greedy, branch-and-bound solver, and simulated annealing. While our approach still does not match the performance of the best classical baseline, it shows promise in a slower runtime scaling with problem size given a fixed budget. This suggests a regime of large problems where subspace sampling on quantum devices could become competitive, as we also demonstrate how improvements in hardware will lead to better algorithm performance. QSSD is thus a practical heuristic for combinatorial optimization problems that helps bring quantum optimization a step closer to utility.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum Subspace Sampling Descent (QSSD) tackles optimization problems larger than the device’s qubit count by iteratively sampling low-energy subspaces while retaining global problem information.
infographic.engineering_relevance: QSSD offers a hardware-tested route to larger combinatorial optimization workloads without requiring one qubit per problem variable.
method: Iteratively search subspaces to decouple variable count from qubit count.
Use fixed-angle QAOA as a low-energy sampler to drive energy descent.
Precompute angles so each iteration requires one circuit execution.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on IBM Heron and Nighthawk devices with up to 152 qubits covered higher-order binary optimization and Max-cut; a 10,000-variable instance achieved an approximation ratio above 0.95 with 100 circuit executions.
infographic.watch_item: QSSD does not yet match the best classical baseline; its reported runtime-scaling promise does not establish quantum advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum optimization beyond qubit count by low-energy subspace sampling

title: THeatA: Transport- and Heating-aware QEC simulation with Cooling Strategies for QCCD Trapped-Ion Systems
authors: Eitaro Ishikawa, Noah Hirai, Koichiro Miyanishi, Hana Ebi, Kazufumi Tanji, Isamu Kudo
abstract: The quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architecture is a promising approach to scalable trapped-ion quantum computing, enabling flexible qubit interactions by transporting ions between dedicated trap zones. Programs for such systems require operations beyond conventional circuit primitives: ion shuttling, physical SWAPs, trap splitting and merging, and cooling. Motional excitation accumulated during transport increases the mean phonon number of ions and degrades the fidelity of the two-qubit Molmer-Sorensen gates. However, existing quantum error correction (QEC) simulation frameworks do not jointly track per-ion motional excitation and explicitly schedule cooling operations with their transport time and heating costs. We develop a full-stack software framework for QEC experiments and simulations on linear QCCD systems with a single ion species, comprising an intermediate representation (IR) supporting QCCD-native operations, a compiler that translates syndrome-extraction circuits into the IR, and a heating-aware noise-injection pipeline that generates noisy Stim circuits. The compiler updates the mean phonon number of each ion throughout the schedule, and the pipeline derives gate-dependent error rates from the tracked phonon states and per-ion timing, enabling the evaluation of finite-size logical-error scaling of the rotated surface code under transport- and heating-aware noise. We show that transport-induced heating prevents logical error rates from decreasing with increasing code distance under the evaluated conditions, and that indirectly cooling the ion pairs involved in two-qubit gates, by merging them with precooled coolant ions immediately before each gate, restores this decrease. By sweeping the duration and post-cooling mean phonon number of an abstract cooling instruction, we characterize their trade-off and identify the region in which logical-error scaling is maintained.

infographic.key_insight: THeatA simulations show that transport-induced heating can prevent logical errors from decreasing with code distance, while cooling ion pairs immediately before two-qubit gates can restore that scaling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: QCCD control and compiler design should account jointly for ion transport, motional heating, and cooling overhead rather than treating gate errors as fixed.
method: Compile syndrome-extraction circuits into an intermediate representation with QCCD-native transport and cooling operations.
Track per-ion mean phonon numbers and timing to generate gate-dependent noise in Stim circuits.
Evaluate rotated surface codes while sweeping cooling duration and post-cooling phonon number.
infographic.evidence_signal: Finite-size simulations identify cooling-parameter regions where logical error rates decrease with increasing code distance under the evaluated transport- and heating-aware noise conditions.
infographic.watch_item: Results are simulation-based for linear, single-species QCCD systems, and the abstract cooling instruction requires validation against realizable cooling protocols.
infographic.paper_title: THeatA: Transport- and Heating-aware QEC simulation with Cooling Strategies for QCCD Trapped-Ion Systems

title: Improving Quantum Oblivious Transfer using Zero-Knowledge Proofs
authors: Alex Bredariol Grilo, Lucas Hanouz, Anne Marin
abstract: While quantum protocols for oblivious transfer can be built from weaker assumptions than classical ones, the current protocols remain highly impractical due to stringent security bounds that demand a large amount of quantum communication. In this work, we propose an enhancement to quantum oblivious transfer protocols by leveraging zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs). At a high level, we modify the protocol such that the receiver proves that they are following honestly some crucial steps of the protocols, without revealing extra information to the sender. This yields a tighter security bound against a malicious receiver. For practical scenarios with a fixed security target, this approach reduces the amount of required quantum communication by one to two orders of magnitude, depending on the specific parameters. Furthermore, the benefits of our approach become particularly pronounced at higher qubit error rates, and our proposal even extends the maximum tolerable error rate of the quantum channel from approximately 3.5% to about 9%. The ZKP, however, introduces a substantial computational overhead, estimated to significantly exceed the acquisition time of the protocol, which is usually the primary bottleneck. To address this limitation, we also introduce a variant that serves as a tunable trade-off between the protocol with and without our modification. This enables precise adjustment of the computational overhead while still retaining significant, albeit moderately reduced, efficiency gains.

infographic.key_insight: Adding zero-knowledge proofs to quantum oblivious transfer can reduce required quantum communication by 10–100× at a fixed security target.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could ease quantum communication requirements and tolerate noisier channels, but shifts substantial cost to classical computation.
method: Require the receiver to prove honest execution of crucial protocol steps without revealing extra information.
Use these proofs to tighten security bounds against malicious receivers.
Introduce a tunable variant that trades computational overhead for communication savings.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports parameter-dependent communication reductions of one to two orders of magnitude and an increase in maximum tolerable channel error rate from approximately 3.5% to 9%.
infographic.watch_item: Estimated proof-computation overhead substantially exceeds quantum acquisition time, potentially outweighing communication savings.
infographic.paper_title: Improving Quantum Oblivious Transfer using Zero-Knowledge Proofs

title: Validity and maximum violation of the entanglement-assisted quantum Singleton bound for linear stabilizer codes
authors: Jae-Hyun Baek, Byung-Sun Won, Jon-Lark Kim
abstract: Entanglement-assisted quantum codes protect quantum information with entangled pairs shared in advance, and the entanglement-assisted quantum Singleton bound of Brun, Devetak and Hsieh is the standard estimate of how many pairs they consume. Codes that violate it at large distance are known. For linear entanglement-assisted stabilizer codes, which include all qubit stabilizer codes of this kind, we determine when the bound holds and how far it can fail. The answer depends on how many qudits, together with the receiver's halves of the pairs, recover the logical qudits. If this number is less than twice the number of logical qudits, the bound holds, also for degenerate codes. If it is exactly twice that, the bound overstates the number of pairs by at most the length of the longest classical maximum distance separable (MDS) code of that dimension, minus the dimension. Codes carrying values and derivatives of polynomials on the projective line attain this maximum whenever the field size is at least that dimension and the MDS conjecture is known for it, which includes every prime and, by a recently announced result, every even field size. If the number is more than twice the number of logical qudits, the violation is bounded in terms of the lengths of classical codes of a given Singleton defect, and the bound is attained for one logical qudit. Apart from cited MDS lengths, the proofs are formalized in the Lean proof assistant.

infographic.key_insight: For linear entanglement-assisted stabilizer codes, the standard quantum Singleton bound holds or can be violated depending on the recovery-set size relative to twice the number of logical qudits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results clarify when the standard bound reliably estimates shared-entanglement requirements and when code designs can consume fewer entangled pairs than it predicts.
method: Classify validity and violation by the number of qudits needed for recovery together with the receiver’s entangled-pair halves.
Bound violations using classical MDS code lengths and codes with specified Singleton defect.
Construct extremal codes from polynomial values and derivatives on the projective line.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical bounds, constructions attaining them in specified regimes, and Lean-formalized proofs apart from cited MDS lengths, rather than hardware experiments.
infographic.watch_item: Maximum-violation attainability depends on field size and applicable classical code-length results; practical implementation costs are not evaluated.
infographic.paper_title: Validity and maximum violation of the entanglement-assisted quantum Singleton bound for linear stabilizer codes

title: Quantum Coherence and Basis-Dependent Correlations in Quantum Systems
authors: Zi-Han Chen, Hui Zhao, Shao-Ming Fei, Zhi-Xi Wang, Mei-Ming Zhang
abstract: Quantum coherence and quantum correlations are two fundamental features of quantum systems and are closely related in various quantum information tasks. In general, due to the existence of correlations, the amount of coherence in a bipartite state should be no less than that in the reduced states. We focus on what types of states have an equal amount of coherence in the global state and the local states. For such states, the basis-dependent correlations (the difference between the coherence of a bipartite state and its reduced state with respect to a set of standard orthogonal local bases) vanish. Based on the Tsallis relative entropy coherence measure, we prove that block-diagonal product states exhibit vanishing basis-dependent correlations. Furthermore, we establish an equivalence between the absence of basis-dependent correlations and the block-diagonal product structure in a special case. We then consider the coherence measure based on quantum Fisher information and show that block?diagonal product states again lead to vanishing basis-dependent correlations, while in the two-qubit case the vanishing condition constrains the state to a broader block-diagonal-like product structure. These results provide a structural characterization of bipartite states with vanishing basis-dependent correlations under different coherence measures.

infographic.key_insight: Block-diagonal product states have vanishing basis-dependent correlations under both Tsallis-relative-entropy and quantum-Fisher-information coherence measures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These structural criteria may help analyze how coherence is distributed across composite quantum systems, rather than directly improve quantum hardware.
method: Compare bipartite and reduced-state coherence in fixed local orthogonal bases.
Prove vanishing correlations for block-diagonal product states using Tsallis relative entropy.
Extend the analysis to quantum Fisher information and characterize two-qubit constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical proofs and special-case structural characterizations, with no experimental data or numerical benchmarks described.
infographic.watch_item: Converse characterizations depend on the coherence measure and apply only in specified special cases; basis choice also matters.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Coherence and Basis-Dependent Correlations in Quantum Systems

title: Large-Scale Streaming Portfolio Optimization with Pauli Correlation Encoding
authors: Vicente P. Soloviev, Josh Kirsopp
abstract: Classical portfolio construction over large asset universes is a combinatorial selection problem that existing heuristics do not solve well at scale. Pauli Correlation Encoding (PCE) addresses this by representing the underlying clustering problem with far fewer qubits than one per asset, and a prior study showed it is competitive with classical methods on a single historical snapshot. This paper moves beyond that static test to a streaming deployment, in which the correlation structure and the portfolio are both re-estimated on a rolling basis, as a live rebalancing system would actually operate. We introduce two streaming variants -- PCE itself and a joint multi-cut variant, dPCE -- and evaluate both against a Buy & Hold baseline across window lengths, portfolio sizes up to several thousand assets, risk-aversion and transaction-cost settings, and measurement-shot budgets. Streaming PCE and dPCE consistently outperform the passive baseline, including during a market downturn where both lose money but PCE loses markedly less -- evidence that the method's value is not confined to rising markets. PCE also proves the more practical choice at scale, since dPCE's resource requirements and its sensitivity to rebalancing frequency both grow faster with portfolio size. We further report which operational choices -- rebalancing cadence, shot budget, and transaction-cost awareness -- matter most for a real deployment, and which matter less than commonly assumed.

infographic.key_insight: Streaming Pauli Correlation Encoding (PCE) outperforms Buy & Hold in the reported evaluations while using far fewer qubits than one per asset.
infographic.engineering_relevance: PCE offers a more practical scaling path than joint multi-cut dPCE for rolling portfolio rebalancing, with lower resource growth and less sensitivity to rebalancing frequency.
method: Encode asset-correlation clustering with Pauli correlations to reduce qubit requirements.
Re-estimate correlations and portfolios on rolling windows using PCE and joint multi-cut dPCE.
Vary rebalancing cadence, risk aversion, transaction costs, and measurement-shot budgets.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across tests with portfolios up to several thousand assets, both streaming variants consistently beat Buy & Hold; during a downturn, PCE lost markedly less than the baseline.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish quantum advantage over strong active classical strategies or specify quantum hardware execution conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Large-Scale Streaming Portfolio Optimization with Pauli Correlation Encoding

title: When Randomness Hides Quantum Simulation Errors
authors: Yue Cao, Tianfeng Feng, Jonathan Allcock, Chenfeng Cao, Qi Zhao
abstract: Trotter formulas approximate quantum dynamics by discrete steps, but errors in measured observables can be much smaller than worst-case estimates. We investigate how this suppression depends on the degree of randomness in the input states. We show that the mean absolute observable-error bound for state 2-designs can be exponentially smaller in qubit number than the tight bound for state 1-designs. To characterize this error transition from 1-design to 2-design, we use the excess frame potential to quantify the ensemble's second-moment distance. We quantify departures from these random-state statistics through the frame potential, a measure of pairwise state overlaps, and identify the accessible observables most sensitive to the resulting deviations in mean-square error. Extending the analysis to a Hamiltonian trajectory whose frame potential decays as $1/T$ before saturation, we also obtain a sufficient $p$th-order Trotter number $\mathcal O(T^{1+3/(4p)})$ for evolution time $T$. These findings connect input-state statistics to the visibility of Trotter errors, giving a theoretical guarantee and foundation for practical quantum simulation.

infographic.key_insight: Input-state randomness can hide Trotter errors: the mean absolute observable-error bound for state 2-designs can be exponentially smaller in qubit count than the tight bound for state 1-designs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accounting for input-state statistics can sharpen quantum-simulation error estimates beyond worst-case bounds.
method: Compare observable-error bounds for state 1-designs and 2-designs.
Use excess frame potential to quantify second-moment deviations and identify sensitive accessible observables.
Extend the analysis to Hamiltonian trajectories with frame potential decaying as 1/T before saturation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical bounds, including a sufficient pth-order Trotter step count of O(T^(1+3/(4p))) under the stated trajectory behavior, rather than experimental benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The improved bounds depend on ensemble randomness and trajectory assumptions; they do not guarantee equally small errors for arbitrary inputs or observables.
infographic.paper_title: When Randomness Hides Quantum Simulation Errors

title: Trotterized hybrid qubit-boson simulation of the Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard model
authors: Nabaraj Khatri, Dilip Ojha, Rajib Tripathi, Kismat K. C, Ashish Khanal
abstract: The Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard (JCH) model describes the interaction of light and matter in coupled optical cavities and provides a framework for studying their quantum dynamics. In this work, we design a Trotterized quantum circuit to investigate the real-time dynamics of the JCH model using Bosonic Qiskit and a Matrix Product State (MPS) backend. We simulate single-polariton transport and benchmark site occupations against exact diagonalization results. We then extend the simulations to the two-excitation sector under a hard-core photon constraint, examining excitation transport and symmetry properties. Finally, we study the dependence of bipartite entanglement entropy on the inter-cavity photon-hopping strength. The results illustrate how hybrid qubit-boson circuits, simulated with matrix product states, can be used to study light-matter lattice dynamics. This work provides a numerical benchmark for extending hybrid simulation approaches to more complex interacting and open light-matter systems.

infographic.key_insight: Trotterized hybrid qubit-boson circuits simulate light-matter transport and entanglement dynamics in the Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach provides a numerical benchmark for developing hybrid quantum simulations of coupled cavities and more complex light-matter systems.
method: Build Trotterized circuits in Bosonic Qiskit with a matrix product state backend.
Simulate single-polariton transport and two-excitation dynamics under a hard-core photon constraint.
Study bipartite entanglement entropy versus inter-cavity photon-hopping strength.
infographic.evidence_signal: Single-polariton site occupations are benchmarked against exact diagonalization; the abstract reports no quantitative error metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The hard-core photon constraint restricts the two-excitation study, so its results should not be generalized to unrestricted photon occupancy.
infographic.paper_title: Trotterized hybrid qubit-boson simulation of the Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard model

title: Reducing RSA-2048 Factoring Resources Below One Billion Toffolis via LLM-Driven Verifiable Quantum Compilation
authors: Xiaodi Li, Yuqing Wang, Xue Chen, Yang-Yang Tang, Linghui Chen, Tao Zhang
abstract: Modular exponentiation dominates the logical cost of factoring 2048-bit RSA integers (RSA-2048) with Shor's algorithm. Recent approaches based on approximate residue number systems (RNS) sharply reduce the required logical qubits, yet still demand billions of Toffoli gates. Optimizing these circuits is difficult because shared ancilla qubits and measurement-based uncomputation tightly couple the arithmetic stages, while rare overflows in compressed registers occur too infrequently for random simulation to detect. Here we use large language model (LLM)-driven search to redesign the RNS pipeline across stages and build a deterministic compiler that produces a Pareto frontier of RSA-2048 circuits. We bound rare overflow probabilities analytically and verify the resulting elementary gate sequences across all constituent RNS primes on representative circuits. Relative to Gidney's 2025 baseline under matched adder accounting, our frontier cuts the minimum qubit-Toffoli product by 70.1% and lowers expected factoring Toffolis by up to 78.6% at matched accumulator precision, bringing RSA-2048 factoring below one billion Toffolis for the first time.

infographic.key_insight: LLM-driven, verifiable compilation redesigns Shor’s arithmetic pipeline to bring expected RSA-2048 factoring costs below one billion Toffoli gates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The resulting circuit frontier offers lower logical resource costs, with trade-offs between qubit count and Toffoli count.
method: Use LLM-driven search to redesign arithmetic stages in an approximate residue number system.
Compile circuit candidates deterministically into a qubit–Toffoli Pareto frontier.
Bound rare overflows analytically and verify elementary gate sequences on representative circuits.
infographic.evidence_signal: Against Gidney’s 2025 baseline with matched adder accounting, the abstract reports a 70.1% reduction in minimum qubit–Toffoli product and up to 78.6% fewer expected factoring Toffolis at matched accumulator precision.
infographic.watch_item: These logical resource savings do not establish practical runtime or physical-qubit requirements on fault-tolerant hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Reducing RSA-2048 Factoring Resources Below One Billion Toffolis via LLM-Driven Verifiable Quantum Compilation

title: Impact of structured noise on bosonic quantum error correction
authors: Guoyu Shu, Ling Hu, Hongbo Wu, Zhongchu Ni, Yanyan Cai, Xiaowei Deng
abstract: Bosonic quantum error correction relies on an accurate description of single-photon loss dissipation using an ideal annihilation operator, under which correctable loss errors act equivalently on different logical code states. In realistic weakly nonlinear bosonic modes, however, coupling to a structured environment can render photon loss Fock-state dependent, thereby modifying the effective dissipation operator and deforming the associated error space. Here, we experimentally investigate this effect in a three-dimensional circuit quantum electrodynamics system. By injecting spectrally engineered environmental noise into a weakly nonlinear oscillator, we observe pronounced frequency selectivity in the measured Fock-state dynamics. While the long-time transition rates converge to the Markovian limit, the transient dynamics display distinctly non-Markovian behavior, in quantitative agreement with a second-order time-convolutionless theory. By applying narrowband noise to a binomially encoded logical qubit, we further demonstrate Fock-state-dependent dissipation channels that drive logical states beyond the nominally correctable error space. These results establish structured environmental noise as a mechanism for deforming photon-loss errors in weakly nonlinear bosonic systems and highlight the need to incorporate realistic, state-dependent dissipation into the design and characterization of bosonic quantum error correction.

infographic.key_insight: Structured environmental noise can make photon loss Fock-state dependent, pushing bosonic logical states outside the nominally correctable error space.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Bosonic quantum error correction should account for realistic environmental spectra and state-dependent dissipation rather than assume an ideal photon-loss operator.
method: Inject spectrally engineered noise into a weakly nonlinear oscillator in a 3D circuit-QED system.
Measure Fock-state dynamics and compare with second-order time-convolutionless theory.
Apply narrowband noise to a binomially encoded logical qubit to probe error-space deformation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Measured dynamics showed frequency-selective loss and non-Markovian transients consistent with theory, while narrowband noise drove encoded states beyond the nominally correctable error space.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify logical error-rate penalties under naturally occurring environmental noise.
infographic.paper_title: Impact of structured noise on bosonic quantum error correction
